title: A hippie on the Ellington bus and the trip to Ethiopia
summary: Asked about fitting in with older black musicians, he says he was a long-haired hippie, never judged, and recalls Barrie Lee Hall, Cootie Williams and the palace of Haile Selassie.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was there any, the feeling of a white boy fitting in with some of these older black men?

You know I was just so crazy in a way, I was just like wow. And when I got the gig with Ellington. I was a hippie. I weighed probably about 65 pounds, not like I do now, and my hair was way down here.

On the bus I was a mess. I was a hippie. But you know they had the white dinner jackets, I was fine on the bandstand. You would do a ponytail this way. They never judged me. You know, if they did they sure kept it quiet. We went to Ethiopia, we went to Haile Selassie’s palace, and there were like, there was like Barrie Lee Hall, you know who he is, a great trumpet player. Barrie Lee Hall. He sat at the feet of Cootie Williams and learned how to play. He was at the totally into Woody Shaw and Freddy and he joined the Cootie taught him, just by being next to him. Anita Hall, who passed, was a great singer, and Rocky White, the drummer. They called us the Mod Squad. And they had to go out and dig up jackets for us to go to the palace.
No kidding. You weren’t ready for that.
I’m a lot different now. I’ve learned, since I’ve been booking my band for years and stuff, but I was a hippie.
